name: Galactomyces ferment filtrate
lead: Galactomyces ferment filtrate (GFF) is a cosmetic ingredient obtained from the fermentation of sake using Galactomyces yeast strains. It is marketed under trade names such as Pitera and is used in brightening and hydrating essences, especially in Japanese and Korean skincare [1][2].

Its use is traced to the observation that the hands of sake brewers, who work with yeast fermentation, stayed youthful-looking, a story repeated in the scientific literature on the ingredient [3]. Products based on GFF are sold widely around the world [3].

Most research is laboratory work on skin cells plus several cosmetic studies of GFF-containing products on volunteers, including a multi-year longitudinal study. Those product studies test formulations that contain other ingredients, so effects cannot be attributed to GFF alone, and independent controlled trials of GFF in isolation were not found among the sources reviewed.

paras: Sources describe GFF as arising from the fermentation of sake with Galactomyces strains, and the ingredient's popularity is linked to the observation that sake brewers' hands look youthful [1][3]. The specific active molecules are not fully identified; Grokipedia says further work is needed to identify its anti-aging components [1].

GFF is positioned for moisturising, calming, pore-refining and brightening effects. Marketing and secondary sources cite reductions in pores, sebum and blackheads for an essence containing a high concentration of the filtrate, though these figures come from a source whose study design was not verified [1].

Laboratory studies on cultured keratinocytes report that GFF modulates gene expression linked to differentiation, proliferation, anchoring junctions and energy metabolism [4][5][6]. Other in vitro work reports downregulation of the inflammatory cytokine IL-33 through an AHR/IL-37 pathway, alongside the drug tapinarof [7], and altered expression of caspase-14, a protein involved in barrier formation, in 3D epidermis models [8]. One report says GFF potentiates an 'anti-inflammaging' system in keratinocytes [3]. These are cell-based findings, not demonstrations of effects on human skin appearance.

A 2021 report developed a portable facial imaging device and ran two 8-week clinical studies in young Japanese women to examine daily fluctuation in pore area, roughness and redness and to evaluate a GFF-containing antioxidative skin-care formula [9]. A 2023 paper describes an 11-year longitudinal rejuvenation study in which daily use of GFF-containing products for 12 months was reported to reverse facial wrinkles, pigmented spots and roughness [10]. A 2021 study evaluated a combination serum of GFF, dexpanthenol and Centella asiatica for post-acne hyperpigmentation in people with skin of color [11].

All of these examined multi-ingredient products or open-design observation, which limits conclusions about GFF itself. Published reviews or independent randomized trials isolating GFF were not identified among the sources reviewed.
Grokipedia reports non-irritating human patch tests and negative genotoxicity results for GFF, with a stated safe concentration limit, but those figures were not independently verified here [1].

timeline.event: Study reports GFF and other cosmetic natural products alter caspase-14 expression in 3D epidermis models [8].
Eight-week studies of a GFF-containing formula on pores, roughness and redness in Japanese women [9].
Eleven-year longitudinal study of GFF-containing products published [10].

card.summary: Sake-yeast ferment behind brightening essences, with cell-lab data and product studies but few isolated human trials.
card.note: Human studies test multi-ingredient products, so GFF-specific effects are unclear.

quick.overview:
GFF is a filtrate from yeast-fermented sake used in essences for hydration, texture and glow. Its story starts with sake brewers' youthful hands.

Product studies report improvements in pores, roughness and pigmentation, but they involve formulas with other ingredients.
quick.mechanism: Cell studies report changes in keratinocyte differentiation, barrier-related proteins and inflammatory signalling. The exact active compounds are unidentified.
quick.risks: Patch tests are reported as non-irritating in secondary sources. No serious safety signals were found in the sources reviewed, though long-term data are limited.
